about: Authored A&P flashcards (docs/anp-spec.md 8.8): the comparison tables and key facts of the pilot topics, one card per fact. Glossary cards are made at runtime from assets/glossary.json. Each card: id (stable forever; stored as fc:<id>), topic (map topic id), core (core concept ids), level, compare (the comparison table it comes from, if any), front, back, why (the causal reason). The page shows only cards whose topic is built. Checked by scripts/lib/anp-tool-checks/flashcards.mjs.

cards.compare: Sagittal vs frontal vs transverse planes
cards.front: Which plane divides the body into right and left parts?
cards.back: The sagittal plane. A midsagittal plane makes equal halves; a parasagittal plane makes unequal ones.
cards.why: A sagittal plane runs vertically from front to back, so it separates the right side from the left.

cards.compare: Sagittal vs frontal vs transverse planes
cards.front: Which plane divides the body into anterior and posterior parts?
cards.back: The frontal (coronal) plane.
cards.why: It runs vertically from side to side, so everything in front of it is anterior and everything behind it is posterior.

cards.compare: Sagittal vs frontal vs transverse planes
cards.front: Which plane divides the body into superior and inferior parts, and what is the cut surface called?
cards.back: The transverse (horizontal) plane; its cut surface is a cross section.
cards.why: A horizontal cut separates upper from lower, which is why CT slices, taken this way, show the body as stacked cross sections.

cards.front: A patient needs fine soft-tissue detail of the brain with no ionizing radiation. CT or MRI?
cards.back: MRI.
cards.why: MRI builds its images from a magnet and radio waves, so it uses no X-rays, and it shows soft tissue in fine detail. CT uses X-rays and is best for bone, bleeding and speed.

cards.front: Is the wrist proximal or distal to the elbow?
cards.back: Distal.
cards.why: Proximal and distal are measured from where the limb attaches to the trunk. The wrist is farther from the shoulder than the elbow is.

cards.front: In anatomical position, is the thumb medial or lateral to the little finger?
cards.back: Lateral.
cards.why: Anatomical position has the palms facing forward, which puts the thumb on the side away from the midline.

cards.front: Superficial vs deep: what do they describe?
cards.back: Superficial means toward the body surface; deep means away from it.
cards.why: They describe depth, not height, so skin is superficial to muscle anywhere on the body.

cards.front: Ipsilateral vs contralateral?
cards.back: Ipsilateral: on the same side of the body. Contralateral: on the opposite side.
cards.why: Both compare sides relative to the midline, so the right hand and left foot are contralateral.

cards.front: Describe anatomical position.
cards.back: Standing upright, facing forward, feet flat and slightly apart, arms at the sides with the palms facing forward.
cards.why: Every directional term is defined from this one fixed pose, so a description stays correct whatever position the body is actually in.

cards.front: Nephrectomy vs nephrostomy: which leaves the kidney in place?
cards.back: Nephrostomy: it makes an opening from the kidney to the outside.
cards.why: -ectomy means cutting out (removal); -ostomy means making an opening. -tomy alone is just cutting into.

cards.front: List the levels of organization from smallest to largest.
cards.back: Chemical, cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism.
cards.why: Each level is built from the one below it: molecules make cells, similar cells make tissues, two or more tissues make an organ.

cards.front: What two cavities make up the dorsal body cavity, and what do they hold?
cards.back: The cranial cavity (brain) and the vertebral canal (spinal cord).
cards.why: Both are enclosed by bone, which is why the organs of the nervous system that they hold are well protected.

cards.front: What separates the thoracic cavity from the abdominopelvic cavity?
cards.back: The diaphragm.
cards.why: The diaphragm is a dome of muscle across the trunk, so it forms the floor of the thoracic cavity and the roof of the abdominopelvic cavity.

cards.front: Four quadrants vs nine regions: how is each grid drawn?
cards.back: Quadrants: one vertical and one horizontal line through the navel. Regions: two vertical and two horizontal lines, like a tic-tac-toe grid.
cards.why: The four quadrants are quick for describing where pain is; the nine regions are finer, so they place organs more precisely.

cards.front: Name the middle column of the nine abdominal regions, from top to bottom.
cards.back: Epigastric, umbilical, hypogastric (pubic).
cards.why: Epi- means above and gastr- means stomach; the umbilical region surrounds the navel; hypo- means below.

cards.compare: Ionic vs covalent vs hydrogen bonds
cards.front: Ionic vs covalent bond: what happens to the electrons?
cards.back: Ionic: electrons are transferred, making a cation and an anion. Covalent: electrons are shared in pairs.
cards.why: Transfer leaves two full, opposite charges that attract; sharing holds two nuclei around the same electron pair.

cards.compare: Ionic vs covalent vs hydrogen bonds
cards.front: What holds a hydrogen bond together?
cards.back: The attraction between a partly positive hydrogen and a partly negative oxygen or nitrogen on another molecule or another part of the same one.
cards.why: No electrons are shared or transferred; the partial charges come from unequal sharing inside polar covalent bonds.

cards.compare: Ionic vs covalent vs hydrogen bonds
cards.front: In the watery inside of your body, which bond type stays strong: ionic, covalent or hydrogen?
cards.back: Covalent.
cards.why: Water molecules surround and separate ions, which weakens ionic bonds, and hydrogen bonds break and re-form constantly. A shared electron pair is not pulled apart by water.

cards.front: Blood left standing in a tube separates. Which part of blood behaves as a suspension?
cards.back: The blood cells.
cards.why: They are large enough to settle out under gravity. Dissolved ions stay evenly spread as a true solution, and very large molecules stay dispersed without settling.

cards.front: Exergonic vs endergonic: which needs to be paired with another reaction to proceed?
cards.back: Endergonic.
cards.why: Its products hold more energy than its reactants, so the energy has to come from an energy-releasing (exergonic) reaction, usually ATP breakdown.

cards.front: Catabolism vs anabolism: which builds large molecules, and which usually releases energy?
cards.back: Anabolism builds large molecules (and takes in energy); catabolism breaks them down and usually releases energy.
cards.why: Joining small units stores energy in new bonds; breaking large molecules into lower-energy products frees it.

cards.front: When NAD+ becomes NADH, is NAD+ oxidized or reduced?
cards.back: Reduced.
cards.why: Reduction means gaining electrons, and in body chemistry that usually comes with hydrogen. NAD+ picks up both.

cards.front: What does an enzyme change about a reaction, and what does it leave unchanged?
cards.back: It lowers the activation energy, so the reaction runs faster. It does not change the energy released or taken in overall, and it is not used up.
cards.why: By holding the reactants in the right position at its active site, the enzyme makes the transition state easier to reach.

cards.compare: Raising the pressure gradient vs lowering the resistance
cards.front: A vessel's radius doubles and the pressure gradient stays the same. What happens to flow?
cards.back: Flow rises about 16-fold.
cards.why: Resistance falls with the fourth power of the radius (2 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 16), and flow equals the pressure gradient divided by resistance.

cards.compare: Raising the pressure gradient vs lowering the resistance
cards.front: The pressure difference along a tube doubles and resistance stays the same. What happens to flow?
cards.back: Flow doubles.
cards.why: Flow is directly proportional to the pressure gradient (flow = pressure gradient / resistance).

cards.front: Write the relationship between flow, pressure gradient and resistance.
cards.back: Flow = pressure gradient / resistance.
cards.why: Fluid moves because pressure is higher at one end; anything that resists the movement (narrow radius, long tube, thick fluid) reduces flow for the same push.

cards.front: pH falls from 7.4 to 6.4. How does the hydrogen ion concentration change?
cards.back: It rises 10-fold.
cards.why: pH is the negative logarithm of the hydrogen ion concentration, so each whole unit down is ten times more hydrogen ions.

cards.front: Acid vs base vs buffer: what does each do?
cards.back: An acid releases hydrogen ions; a base takes them up (or releases hydroxide); a buffer takes up or releases hydrogen ions to resist a change in pH.
cards.why: A buffer is a pair (a weak acid and its partner base), so it can soak up added acid or added base.

cards.front: What is the normal pH range of arterial blood?
cards.why: Hydrogen ions bind to proteins and change their charges, so proteins change shape and stop working outside a narrow pH range. Blood pH is held within these limits.

cards.compare: Diffusion vs osmosis vs bulk flow
cards.front: Diffusion vs osmosis vs bulk flow: what moves, and what drives it?
cards.back: Diffusion: solute moves down its own concentration gradient. Osmosis: water moves across a selectively permeable membrane toward the side with more solute. Bulk flow: whole fluid moves down a pressure gradient.
cards.why: Diffusion comes from random molecular motion. In osmosis, solute the membrane holds back lowers the water pressure in the membrane's pores on its side, so water streams through toward it. Bulk flow moves a whole fluid down a pressure gradient, such as the one the heart creates.

cards.compare: Diffusion vs osmosis vs bulk flow
cards.front: Solute that cannot cross a membrane is added to one side. Which way does water move?
cards.back: Toward the side with the added solute.
cards.why: The solute that cannot cross lowers the water pressure inside the membrane's pores on that side, so water streams through toward it: water follows solute.

cards.front: Voltage vs current in the body?
cards.back: Voltage is a difference in electrical charge between two places. Current is the flow of charge, carried in the body by ions.
cards.why: Separated charge is stored potential energy; it drives a current only where there is a path, such as open pores that let ions cross a membrane.

cards.front: Which ion is high outside cells and which is high inside?
cards.back: Sodium is high outside (about 140 mmol/L); potassium is high inside (about 140 mmol/L).
cards.why: A membrane pump that spends ATP keeps moving sodium out and potassium in, which maintains these opposite gradients.

cards.front: Why can oxygen cross the plasma membrane easily but sodium ions cannot?
cards.back: Oxygen is small and nonpolar, so it dissolves through the hydrophobic core of the bilayer. Charged ions are repelled by that core and need proteins to cross.
cards.why: The phospholipid tails form a water-free middle layer that blocks charged and polar particles.

cards.front: Rough ER vs smooth ER: main jobs?
cards.back: Rough ER: folds and modifies proteins made on its ribosomes. Smooth ER: makes lipids and steroids, breaks down some drugs and stores calcium.
cards.why: Rough ER is studded with ribosomes, so proteins are delivered straight into it; smooth ER has none.

cards.compare: Microfilaments vs intermediate filaments vs microtubules
cards.front: Rank microfilaments, intermediate filaments and microtubules from thinnest to thickest.
cards.back: Microfilaments (about 7 nm), intermediate filaments (about 10 nm), microtubules (about 25 nm).
cards.why: Microfilaments are twisted actin strands, intermediate filaments are rope-like proteins, and microtubules are hollow tubes of tubulin.

cards.compare: Microfilaments vs intermediate filaments vs microtubules
cards.front: Which cytoskeleton fiber is most permanent and best at resisting pulling forces?
cards.back: Intermediate filaments.
cards.why: Their rope-like proteins are tough and are not rapidly built and taken apart, so they hold cells in shape under tension.

cards.front: Cilia vs microvilli: which moves, and which increases surface area?
cards.back: Cilia beat and move fluid across the cell surface. Microvilli do not move; they increase surface area for absorption.
cards.why: Cilia have a microtubule core that motor proteins bend; microvilli have an actin core that only holds their shape.

cards.front: What happens in mitochondria?
cards.back: Most of the cell's ATP is made there, using oxygen.
cards.why: The folded inner membrane holds the proteins that make ATP; its folds give room for many of them.

cards.compare: Tight junction vs desmosome vs gap junction
cards.front: Which junction stops fluid leaking between the cells of the intestine or bladder lining?
cards.back: The tight junction.
cards.why: Claudins and occludin fuse neighboring membranes in a continuous band, so there is no space for fluid to pass between the cells.

cards.compare: Tight junction vs desmosome vs gap junction
cards.front: Which junction keeps skin cells from pulling apart, and what is it tied to inside the cell?
cards.back: The desmosome, tied to intermediate filaments.
cards.why: Cadherins bridge the gap between cells, and intermediate filaments spread the pulling force through each cell.

cards.compare: Tight junction vs desmosome vs gap junction
cards.front: Which junction lets heart cells contract together, and how?
cards.back: The gap junction: connexon tunnels let ions pass directly from cell to cell.
cards.why: Ions carrying an electrical change flow straight into the neighboring cell, so the change spreads through the tissue.

cards.front: Passive vs active transport: direction and energy source?
cards.back: Passive: down a gradient, powered by the gradient itself. Active: against a gradient, powered by ATP directly (primary) or by another gradient (secondary).
cards.why: Moving a substance from low to high concentration takes energy; moving it downhill releases energy.

cards.front: For each ATP it uses, what does the sodium-potassium pump move?
cards.back: 3 sodium ions out and 2 potassium ions in.
cards.why: Both move against their gradients, so the pump uses ATP directly: it is primary active transport.

cards.front: Glucose enters intestinal cells together with sodium, against its own gradient. What powers it?
cards.back: The sodium gradient: this is secondary active transport.
cards.why: Sodium rushing in down its gradient carries glucose with it. The gradient exists only because the sodium-potassium pump spends ATP, so ATP is used indirectly.

cards.compare: Simple vs facilitated diffusion vs channels
cards.front: Why does facilitated diffusion level off at high concentrations while simple diffusion does not?
cards.back: Facilitated diffusion uses a limited number of carrier proteins, which become saturated.
cards.why: Once every carrier is busy, adding more solute cannot speed transport; simple diffusion through the bilayer has no such limit.

cards.front: A red blood cell is placed in a hypotonic solution. What happens?
cards.back: Water enters the cell; it swells and can burst (hemolysis).
cards.why: The solution has less solute that cannot cross than the cell does, so water moves by osmosis into the cell.

cards.front: A red blood cell is placed in a hypertonic solution. What happens?
cards.back: Water leaves the cell; it shrinks and crenates.
cards.why: The outside has more solute that cannot cross, so water moves out of the cell by osmosis.

cards.front: DNA vs RNA: sugar, bases and strands?
cards.back: DNA: deoxyribose; A, T, G, C; two strands. RNA: ribose; A, U, G, C; usually one strand.
cards.why: Uracil replaces thymine in RNA and still pairs with adenine, so RNA can copy a gene's code.

cards.front: Transcription vs translation: what is made, and where?
cards.back: Transcription: an RNA copy of a gene is made in the nucleus. Translation: ribosomes in the cytoplasm read mRNA to build a protein.
cards.why: DNA stays in the nucleus, so a messenger copy has to carry the instructions out to the ribosomes.

cards.front: What is a codon?
cards.back: A sequence of three mRNA bases that stands for one amino acid (or a stop signal).
cards.why: Transfer RNA with the matching three-base anticodon brings the right amino acid to the ribosome.

cards.front: Chromosome vs chromatid?
cards.back: A chromosome is one whole DNA molecule with its proteins. A chromatid is one of the two identical copies of a chromosome after it has been copied, held together until they separate.
cards.why: Copying doubles the DNA molecules; the two copies stay joined as sister chromatids until the cell divides.

cards.front: How many chromosomes are in one of your body cells?
cards.back: 46 (23 pairs).
cards.why: You inherit one set of 23 from each parent.

cards.front: Why must usually both copies of a tumor suppressor gene be mutated, but only one copy of an oncogene?
cards.back: A tumor suppressor is a brake: one working copy still stops division. An oncogene is a stuck accelerator: one overactive copy is enough to push division.
cards.why: Loss of function needs both copies gone; a gain of function shows up even with one normal copy present.

cards.front: In which phase of the cell cycle is DNA copied?
cards.back: The S (synthesis) phase of interphase.
cards.why: The cell must copy all 46 DNA molecules before mitosis so each daughter cell gets a full set.

cards.front: Aerobic vs anaerobic breakdown of one glucose: roughly how much ATP, and what is the end product?
cards.back: Aerobic: about 30 to 32 ATP; carbon dioxide and water. Anaerobic: 2 ATP; lactate.
cards.why: Without oxygen, the electron transport chain stops, so only glycolysis runs. Turning pyruvate into lactate regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can continue.

cards.front: Name the stages of aerobic cellular respiration in order.
cards.back: Glycolysis (cytosol), the citric acid cycle (mitochondria), then the electron transport chain (inner mitochondrial membrane).
cards.why: Glycolysis splits glucose; the citric acid cycle strips its carbons to carbon dioxide and loads NADH; the electron transport chain uses NADH and oxygen to make most of the ATP.

cards.front: Why are the air sacs of the lungs lined with simple squamous epithelium?
cards.back: One layer of flat cells gives the shortest path for gases to diffuse.
cards.why: Diffusion time rises steeply with distance, so the thinnest possible barrier speeds exchange.

cards.front: Keratinized vs nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium: where is each?
cards.back: Keratinized: the epidermis of the skin. Nonkeratinized: moist surfaces such as the mouth, esophagus and vagina.
cards.why: Many layers resist wear; keratin in dead surface cells also resists water loss, which a dry surface needs.

cards.front: Where is transitional epithelium, and what does it allow?
cards.back: In the ureters, bladder and first part of the urethra; it stretches without tearing.
cards.why: Its dome-shaped surface cells flatten as the organ fills, so the lining gets thinner and wider instead of splitting.

cards.front: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium: how many layers, and where?
cards.back: One layer that looks like several; it lines the inside of the nose, the trachea and the larger airways.
cards.why: Every cell touches the basement membrane, but nuclei sit at different heights. Goblet cells make mucus and cilia sweep it out.

cards.front: How does epithelium get oxygen and nutrients if it has no blood vessels?
cards.back: By diffusion from blood vessels in the tissue beneath the basement membrane.
cards.why: Epithelium is avascular, so substances diffuse up from the underlying tissue.

cards.front: Why do tendons heal slowly compared with areolar tissue?
cards.back: Dense connective tissue has a poor blood supply and few cells, mostly fibroblasts.
cards.why: Repair needs delivered nutrients and cells that make new fibers, and tendons have little of either.

cards.front: Dense regular vs dense irregular connective tissue: fiber arrangement and example?
cards.back: Regular: parallel collagen fibers, as in tendons and ligaments. Irregular: fibers in all directions, as in the dermis.
cards.why: Parallel fibers resist pulling in one direction; interwoven fibers resist pulling from any direction.

cards.compare: Hyaline vs fibrocartilage vs elastic cartilage
cards.front: Which cartilage is in intervertebral discs, and why that kind?
cards.back: Fibrocartilage: its thick collagen bundles resist both compression and pulling.
cards.why: Discs are squeezed and pulled as the spine bends, and the thick collagen bundles of fibrocartilage resist both.

cards.compare: Hyaline vs fibrocartilage vs elastic cartilage
cards.front: Which cartilage shapes the ear flap and epiglottis?
cards.back: Elastic cartilage.
cards.why: Its dense web of elastic fibers lets it bend and spring back to shape.

cards.compare: Hyaline vs fibrocartilage vs elastic cartilage
cards.front: Which cartilage covers joint surfaces and forms the rings in the trachea wall?
cards.back: Hyaline cartilage.
cards.why: Its fine collagen fibers make a smooth, glassy, slightly flexible surface that resists compression.

cards.compare: Skeletal vs cardiac vs smooth muscle
cards.front: Which muscle types are striated, and which is voluntary?
cards.back: Skeletal and cardiac are striated. Only skeletal is voluntary.
cards.why: Striations come from regularly lined-up contractile proteins. Voluntary means you decide when it contracts; cardiac and smooth muscle contract without your choosing.

cards.compare: Skeletal vs cardiac vs smooth muscle
cards.front: What joins neighboring cells in cardiac muscle, and what does each part do?
cards.back: Intercalated discs: desmosomes hold the cells together; gap junctions pass the electrical signal from cell to cell.
cards.why: Desmosomes keep the cells from pulling apart as they squeeze, and gap junctions let the electrical change pass straight into the next cell, so the cells contract as a unit.

cards.compare: Skeletal vs cardiac vs smooth muscle
cards.front: Which muscle type repairs itself worst, and what fills the gap?
cards.back: Cardiac muscle; connective tissue fills the gap left by lost fibers.
cards.why: Adult cardiac muscle fibers rarely divide and there are few stem cells beside them, so dead fibers are replaced by connective tissue.

cards.front: Neurons vs neuroglia: what does each do?
cards.back: Neurons carry electrical signals. Neuroglia support, protect and nourish neurons, and some wrap axons in insulating layers.
cards.why: Neurons are the signaling cells; glial cells, about as numerous as neurons overall, keep the environment around them right.

cards.compare: Potassium leak vs the sodium-potassium pump
cards.front: What creates most of the resting membrane potential of about -70 mV?
cards.back: Potassium leaking out through potassium leak channels.
cards.why: As positive potassium ions leave down their gradient, they leave behind large negative molecules that cannot follow, so the inside becomes negative.

cards.compare: Potassium leak vs the sodium-potassium pump
cards.front: If the sodium-potassium pump stopped, would the resting potential vanish at once?
cards.back: No. It shifts only a few millivolts at first, then fades slowly as the gradients run down.
cards.why: The pump contributes only a few millivolts directly; its main job is keeping the sodium and potassium gradients from running down.

cards.front: Graded potential vs action potential: which varies with stimulus size, and which is all-or-none?
cards.back: Graded potentials vary with stimulus size and fade with distance. Action potentials are all-or-none and keep full size along the axon.
cards.why: An action potential is regenerated at each patch of membrane by voltage-gated channels once threshold is reached.

cards.front: Which ion movements make the voltage rise and then fall during an action potential?
cards.back: Rising (depolarization): sodium flows in through voltage-gated sodium channels. Falling (repolarization): potassium flows out through voltage-gated potassium channels.
cards.why: At threshold the sodium channels open first; they then inactivate while slower potassium channels open.

cards.front: Why can two action potentials not add together the way graded potentials can?
cards.back: The refractory period: inactivated sodium channels cannot reopen until the membrane repolarizes.
cards.why: While the sodium channels are inactivated, no stimulus can trigger a new action potential, so each one stays separate.

cards.front: Where is the receptor protein for a lipid-soluble messenger such as a steroid, and why?
cards.back: Inside the cell (cytosol or nucleus), because the messenger diffuses through the phospholipid bilayer.
cards.why: A water-soluble messenger cannot cross the bilayer, so its receptor protein has to be on the cell surface.

cards.front: Why do lipid-soluble messengers act slowly (hours) but last long?
cards.back: They change which genes are expressed, so the cell has to make new proteins.
cards.why: Water-soluble messengers instead change the activity of proteins the cell already has, which takes milliseconds to minutes.

cards.front: Nervous vs endocrine signaling: speed, reach and duration?
cards.back: Nervous: milliseconds, only the cell across each synapse, brief. Endocrine: seconds to hours, every target cell the blood reaches, minutes to days.
cards.why: A neurotransmitter crosses one tiny gap and is cleared fast; a hormone travels in blood to any cell with its receptor protein.

cards.front: Endocrine vs exocrine gland: duct, and where does the product go?
cards.back: Exocrine: has a duct; product goes onto a surface. Endocrine: ductless; product goes into interstitial fluid and then blood.
cards.why: Endocrine glands grow from epithelium that lost its link to the surface, so blood is their only route out.

cards.compare: Merocrine vs apocrine vs holocrine secretion
cards.front: Merocrine, apocrine, holocrine: which destroys the cell?
cards.back: Holocrine: the whole cell breaks apart and becomes the product, as in oil glands of the skin.
cards.why: Merocrine releases only vesicle contents by exocytosis; apocrine loses the apical part of the cell and repairs it.

cards.compare: Mucous vs serous vs cutaneous vs synovial membranes
cards.front: Which body membrane lines a closed body cavity, and what fluid does it make?
cards.back: A serous membrane; it makes serous fluid, which lets organs slide with little friction.
cards.why: Mucous membranes line tracts open to the outside, and synovial membranes line movable joints.

cards.compare: Mucous vs serous vs cutaneous vs synovial membranes
cards.front: Which body membrane has no epithelium?
cards.back: The synovial membrane.
cards.why: It is a connective tissue membrane: its surface is a layer of connective tissue cells, not an epithelium.

cards.front: Necrosis vs apoptosis: which causes inflammation, and why?
cards.back: Necrosis. The cell swells and its membrane ruptures, spilling contents that trigger inflammation.
cards.why: In apoptosis the cell shrinks and is packaged into sealed pieces, so nothing leaks out.

cards.front: Negative vs positive feedback: how does the response relate to the stimulus?
cards.back: Negative feedback opposes the stimulus, returning the variable toward its set point. Positive feedback strengthens the stimulus, driving it further.
cards.why: That is why negative loops switch themselves off and positive loops need an outside event to end them.

cards.front: Give two examples of positive feedback in the body.
cards.back: Childbirth contractions and blood clotting.
cards.why: In both, each step triggers more of itself, so the process speeds up until an end point breaks the loop: delivery of the baby or a finished clot.

cards.front: List the parts of a feedback loop in order.
cards.back: Stimulus, sensory receptor (sensor), afferent pathway, control center, efferent pathway, effector, response.
cards.why: The sensor detects the change and reports it inward (afferent); the control center compares it with the set point and sends commands outward (efferent) to the effector.

cards.front: Body temperature falls. Name the effectors and what they do.
cards.back: Smooth muscle in skin blood vessels constricts them, so less heat is lost; skeletal muscles shiver, releasing heat.
cards.why: Both responses oppose the fall, so this is negative feedback.

cards.front: Fibrous vs serous pericardium: what does each do?
cards.back: Fibrous: tough outer bag that anchors the heart and limits how far it can expand. Serous: two thin layers with serous fluid between them, so the heart slides with little friction.
cards.why: Dense collagen resists stretch; mesothelium secretes the lubricating fluid.

cards.front: Name the three layers of the heart wall from outside in.
cards.back: Epicardium, myocardium, endocardium.
cards.why: The epicardium is the visceral pericardium; the myocardium is the thick cardiac muscle that pumps; the endocardium is the smooth endothelial lining.

cards.front: Where does the heart sit, and where does its apex point?
cards.back: In the mediastinum, between the lungs, just above the diaphragm; the apex points down, forward and to the left.
cards.why: That tilt is why the heartbeat is felt most strongly on the left of the chest.

cards.front: Which valves have chordae tendineae and papillary muscles?
cards.back: The atrioventricular (tricuspid and mitral) valves.
cards.why: When the ventricle squeezes, the papillary muscles pull on the cords so the flaps cannot flip back into the atrium. Semilunar cusps need no cords.

cards.front: Name the four heart valves by side.
cards.back: Right: tricuspid and pulmonary. Left: mitral (bicuspid) and aortic.
cards.why: Each side has one atrioventricular valve and one semilunar valve at the exit to its artery.

cards.front: What opens and closes a heart valve?
cards.back: The pressure difference across it: a valve opens when pressure behind it is higher and closes when pressure ahead of it is higher.
cards.why: Valves are passive flaps; muscle does not push them open.

cards.front: Which vessels enter the left atrium, and what do they carry?
cards.back: The pulmonary veins, usually four, carrying blood that has just picked up oxygen in the lungs.
cards.why: They are veins because they carry blood toward the heart, even though that blood carries plenty of oxygen.

cards.front: Why is the left ventricle wall much thicker than the right?
cards.back: It pumps blood to the whole body, against far more resistance, so it must make about 120 mm Hg, versus about 25 mm Hg for the right, which pumps only through the lungs.
cards.why: Both pump the same volume per minute, but the left must generate far more pressure to push it through the whole body.

cards.front: Pulmonary vs systemic circuit: which pump, and which kind of blood do their arteries carry?
cards.back: Pulmonary: right ventricle; its arteries carry deoxygenated blood. Systemic: left ventricle; its arteries carry oxygenated blood.
cards.why: Arteries are named for direction (away from the heart), not for oxygen content.

cards.front: Over a minute, does the right ventricle pump more, less or the same volume as the left?
cards.back: The same.
cards.why: The two circuits are in series, so whatever one side pumps out must come back to the other; a lasting mismatch would pool blood in one circuit.

cards.front: Trace blood from the venae cavae to the aorta.
cards.back: Right atrium, tricuspid valve, right ventricle, pulmonary valve, pulmonary trunk and arteries, lungs, pulmonary veins, left atrium, mitral valve, left ventricle, aortic valve, aorta.
cards.why: Each valve opens only forward, so the pressure the ventricles build moves blood one way through both circuits.

cards.front: Angina vs myocardial infarction: which raises troponin in the blood, and why?
cards.back: Myocardial infarction: ischemia lasts long enough to kill heart muscle, and dying cells release troponin.
cards.why: In angina the ischemia reverses before cells die, so no troponin leaks out.

cards.front: When does most blood flow through the left ventricle's coronary vessels, and why?
cards.back: During diastole, when the relaxed muscle stops squeezing the vessels inside the wall.
cards.why: Contraction compresses the vessels in the ventricle wall, raising their resistance; relaxation lowers it.

cards.compare: Skeletal vs cardiac muscle action potential
cards.front: Why is a ventricular muscle action potential about 100 times longer than a skeletal muscle one?
cards.back: It has a plateau: calcium flows in through slow (L-type) calcium channels while potassium flows out, holding the membrane depolarized.
cards.why: The inward calcium roughly balances the outward potassium for about 200 milliseconds before repolarization wins.

cards.compare: Skeletal vs cardiac muscle action potential
cards.front: Why can the heart not go into a sustained (tetanic) contraction?
cards.back: Its refractory period lasts almost as long as the contraction itself.
cards.why: A new action potential cannot start until the muscle is relaxing, so contractions cannot fuse and the ventricles always get time to refill.

cards.compare: Skeletal vs cardiac muscle action potential
cards.front: How does calcium from outside the cell trigger cardiac muscle contraction?
cards.back: Calcium entering during the plateau opens calcium release channels on the sarcoplasmic reticulum, releasing much more calcium (calcium-induced calcium release).
cards.why: In skeletal muscle the release channels are opened mechanically by the voltage sensor instead, so outside calcium is not needed.

cards.compare: Contractile cell vs pacemaker cell action potential
cards.front: Why does a pacemaker cell fire on its own while a contractile cell does not?
cards.back: A pacemaker cell has no stable resting potential: an inward sodium current through HCN channels (the funny current) and then calcium entry slowly depolarize it to threshold.
cards.why: A contractile cell rests steadily near -90 mV until a neighbor's current reaches it through gap junctions.

cards.compare: Contractile cell vs pacemaker cell action potential
cards.front: Which ion causes the rapid upstroke of a pacemaker cell action potential, and which causes it in a contractile cell?
cards.back: Pacemaker: calcium (through L-type calcium channels). Contractile: sodium (through fast voltage-gated sodium channels).
cards.why: Pacemaker cells sit too depolarized for their fast sodium channels to work, so calcium channels carry the upstroke, which is why it is slower.

cards.front: Trace the conduction pathway of the heart.
cards.back: SA node, atrial muscle, AV node, AV bundle (bundle of His), right and left bundle branches, Purkinje fibers, ventricular muscle.
cards.why: The SA node fires fastest, so it sets the pace; the rest of the path spreads the signal so the atria contract before the ventricles.

cards.front: What does the AV nodal delay of about 0.1 second do?
cards.back: It holds the signal back, so the atria finish contracting and top up the ventricles before the ventricles are excited.
cards.why: AV nodal cells are small, have few gap junctions and a slow calcium-driven upstroke, so conduction through them is slow.

cards.front: Intrinsic firing rates: SA node, AV node and AV bundle, bundle branches and Purkinje fibers?
cards.back: SA node about 100 per minute with no nerve input (60 to 100 at rest); AV node and AV bundle about 40 to 60; bundle branches and Purkinje fibers about 20 to 40.
cards.why: The fastest pacemaker resets the others each beat, so a slower backup takes over only if the faster one fails.

cards.front: What does each ECG wave record: P, QRS, T?
cards.back: P: atrial depolarization. QRS: ventricular depolarization. T: ventricular repolarization.
cards.why: Atrial repolarization happens during the QRS complex, so the larger ventricular signal hides it.

cards.front: What does a long PR interval (over 0.20 s) tell you?
cards.back: Conduction from the atria to the ventricles is slowed, mostly at the AV node.
cards.why: The PR interval runs from the start of atrial depolarization to the start of ventricular depolarization, so it measures the AV delay.

cards.front: Does an ECG show the heart contracting?
cards.back: No. It shows electrical changes; contraction follows them shortly after.
cards.why: Depolarization triggers contraction, but a heart can show electrical activity with no effective pumping.

cards.front: What causes the first (S1) and second (S2) heart sounds?
cards.back: S1: the AV valves closing as the ventricles start to contract. S2: the semilunar valves closing as the ventricles relax.
cards.why: The sound is not the thin cusps slapping together. The closing valve suddenly stops the moving blood, which sets the blood, the cusps and the chamber walls vibrating.

cards.front: During isovolumetric contraction, why does ventricular volume not change?
cards.back: All four valves are closed: ventricular pressure is above atrial pressure but still below arterial pressure.
cards.why: Blood can leave only once ventricular pressure passes aortic (or pulmonary) pressure and the semilunar valves open.

cards.front: End-diastolic volume is 120 mL and end-systolic volume is 50 mL. What are the stroke volume and ejection fraction?
cards.back: Stroke volume 70 mL; ejection fraction about 58%.
cards.why: Stroke volume = EDV - ESV = 70 mL; ejection fraction = SV / EDV = 70 / 120.

cards.front: How do the ventricles mostly fill: by atrial contraction or passively?
cards.back: Mostly passively (about 70 to 80%) while the AV valves are open; atrial contraction adds the rest.
cards.why: Blood returning to the atria flows straight on into the relaxed ventricles down the pressure gradient.

cards.front: Arteries vs capillaries vs veins: wall structure?
cards.back: Arteries: thick walls with a thick muscular or elastic middle layer (tunica media). Capillaries: endothelium on a basement membrane only. Veins: thin walls, wide lumen, valves in the limbs.
cards.why: Arteries must withstand high pressure; capillaries must be thin for exchange; veins carry low-pressure blood and need valves to stop it flowing back.

cards.front: Where is most of your blood at rest?
cards.back: In the systemic veins and venules, about 60 to 65%.
cards.why: Their thin walls stretch easily, so they hold a large volume at low pressure, a reserve that sympathetic venoconstriction can shift toward the heart.

cards.front: Which vessels set how much blood enters a capillary bed?
cards.back: The arterioles, by constricting or dilating their smooth muscle.
cards.why: Small changes in their radius change resistance by the fourth power. Whether discrete precapillary sphincters do this in humans is unsettled; many exams still name them.

cards.front: How do the elastic arteries keep blood flowing during diastole?
cards.back: Their walls stretch during ejection and recoil during diastole, pushing blood onward.
cards.why: Elastic fibers store some of the energy of each heartbeat and release it between beats, smoothing flow.

cards.front: Name the three branches of the aortic arch in order.
cards.back: Brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid artery, left subclavian artery.
cards.why: On the right, the brachiocephalic trunk splits into the right common carotid and right subclavian, so the right side has one extra step.

cards.front: Name the three unpaired branches of the abdominal aorta that supply the gut.
cards.back: Celiac trunk, superior mesenteric artery, inferior mesenteric artery.
cards.why: They leave the front of the aorta from top to bottom, supplying the upper, middle and lower digestive tract.

cards.front: Where do the coronary arteries begin?
cards.back: At the base of the ascending aorta, just above the aortic valve.
cards.why: They are the first branches of the aorta, so the heart muscle gets freshly oxygenated blood.

cards.front: What drains into the superior vena cava vs the inferior vena cava?
cards.back: Superior: head, neck, upper limbs and upper chest. Inferior: the body below the diaphragm.
cards.why: Both empty into the right atrium, along with the coronary sinus from the heart wall.

cards.front: Why does blood from the stomach and intestines go to the liver before the heart?
cards.back: The hepatic portal vein carries it through a second capillary bed in the liver.
cards.why: The liver can process absorbed nutrients and remove drugs and toxins before the blood reaches the rest of the body.

cards.front: Which vein drains most blood from the brain?
cards.back: The internal jugular vein.
cards.why: Blood from the brain collects in dural venous sinuses, which empty into the internal jugular veins.

cards.front: Blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg. Estimate the mean arterial pressure and the pulse pressure.
cards.back: MAP about 93 mm Hg; pulse pressure 40 mm Hg.
cards.why: Pulse pressure = systolic - diastolic. At rest the heart spends about two thirds of each cycle in diastole, so MAP is about diastolic + one third of the pulse pressure.

cards.front: Where along the systemic circuit does blood pressure fall the most?
cards.back: Across the arterioles.
cards.why: They are the main resistance vessels, and pressure falls most where resistance is highest.

cards.front: Why does blood move slowest in the capillaries?
cards.back: Their total cross-sectional area is the largest of any vessel type.
cards.why: The same flow spread over a much larger total area moves more slowly, which gives time for exchange.

cards.front: Heart rate is 70 beats/min and stroke volume is 70 mL. What is cardiac output?
cards.back: About 4.9 L/min.
cards.why: Cardiac output = heart rate x stroke volume = 70 x 70 mL = 4,900 mL per minute.

cards.front: Name the three factors that set stroke volume.
cards.back: Preload (how much the ventricle is stretched by filling), contractility, and afterload (the pressure it must overcome to eject).
cards.why: More stretch or more contractility raises stroke volume; higher afterload lowers it.

cards.front: Venous return increases. Why does stroke volume rise with no nerve or hormone signal?
cards.back: The Frank-Starling mechanism: more filling stretches the muscle fibers toward a better length, so they contract more strongly.
cards.why: This matches the output of the heart to what returns to it, beat by beat, and keeps the two ventricles in balance.

cards.front: Sympathetic vs parasympathetic effects on the heart?
cards.back: Sympathetic: raises heart rate and contractility. Parasympathetic (vagus nerves): lowers heart rate, with little effect on ventricular contractility.
cards.why: Vagal fibers go mainly to the SA and AV nodes, while sympathetic fibers also reach the ventricular muscle.

cards.front: Baroreceptor reflex vs atrial reflex: what does more stretch do to heart rate?
cards.back: Baroreceptor reflex (arterial stretch): heart rate falls. Atrial reflex (atrial stretch from filling): heart rate rises.
cards.why: The first opposes changes in arterial pressure. In the second, stretch of the atrial wall speeds the SA node, so the heart pumps on more of the returning blood. In people this reflex is modest and often masked by the baroreceptor reflex.

cards.front: You stand up quickly and blood pressure drops. What does the baroreceptor reflex do?
cards.back: Less stretch lowers baroreceptor firing, so the brainstem raises sympathetic output and lowers vagal output: heart rate, contractility and arteriolar constriction all rise.
cards.why: Each change raises cardiac output or resistance, and mean arterial pressure = cardiac output x resistance.

cards.compare: Short-term vs long-term blood pressure control
cards.front: Short-term vs long-term blood pressure control: what does each adjust, and how fast?
cards.back: Short-term (baroreceptor reflex): heart rate, contractility and vessel diameter, within seconds. Long-term (kidneys and hormones): blood volume, over hours to days.
cards.why: Baroreceptors reset to a sustained new pressure within days, so lasting control depends on the kidneys changing how much salt and water they keep.

cards.front: Blood pressure falls. How does the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system raise it?
cards.back: The kidneys release renin; angiotensin II forms, which constricts arterioles and triggers aldosterone release; aldosterone makes the kidneys keep sodium, and water follows.
cards.why: Constriction raises resistance quickly; keeping sodium and water raises blood volume over hours to days.

cards.front: The atria are overstretched by high blood volume. Which hormone do they release, and what does it do?
cards.back: Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP): the kidneys lose more sodium and water, and vessels dilate.
cards.why: Losing sodium and water lowers blood volume, which reduces the stretch that triggered the release.

cards.front: Which two forces mainly push fluid out of and pull fluid into a capillary?
cards.back: Out: capillary hydrostatic (blood) pressure. In: the colloid osmotic pressure of plasma proteins.
cards.why: Blood pressure pushes water through the capillary wall; plasma proteins cannot cross easily, so they hold water in by osmosis.

cards.front: In most capillary beds at steady state, is fluid reabsorbed at the venous end?
cards.back: Current evidence says mostly not: filtration exceeds reabsorption along most of the length, and a separate set of thin drainage vessels returns the excess fluid to the blood. Many exams still expect the classic answer: filtration at the arterial end, reabsorption at the venous end.
cards.why: The glycocalyx on the endothelium keeps the fluid just under it low in protein, so the effective inward pull is weaker than the old model assumed.

cards.front: Name four causes of edema.
cards.back: Raised capillary hydrostatic pressure (as when a failing heart backs blood up into the veins), low plasma proteins (as in liver disease), leaky capillaries (inflammation), and blocked drainage of excess tissue fluid.
cards.why: Each one either increases filtration out of the capillaries or stops the extra fluid from being drained back to the blood.

cards.front: Name the four main types of shock and the problem in each.
cards.back: Hypovolemic: too little blood volume. Cardiogenic: the heart fails to pump. Distributive (septic, anaphylactic, neurogenic): widespread vasodilation. Obstructive: something blocks filling or outflow, such as a clot in the lungs.
cards.why: Each lowers either cardiac output or resistance, so mean arterial pressure and tissue perfusion fall.

cards.front: Why does neurogenic shock cause a slow heart rate with warm skin, unlike hypovolemic shock?
cards.back: Loss of sympathetic output: vessels dilate (warm skin) and nothing speeds the heart, so vagal input slows it.
cards.why: In hypovolemic shock the sympathetic system works, so it constricts skin vessels (cool, pale skin) and raises heart rate.

cards.front: Left-sided vs right-sided heart failure: where does blood back up, and what do you see?
cards.back: Left: into the lungs, causing shortness of breath and crackles. Right: into the systemic veins, causing swollen neck veins, leg edema and an enlarged liver.
cards.why: A failing ventricle cannot move on what flows into it, so pressure rises in the veins that feed it.

cards.front: What is the most common cause of right-sided heart failure?
cards.back: Left-sided heart failure.
cards.why: Blood backing up into the lungs raises pulmonary pressure, and the right ventricle fails against that higher afterload.

cards.front: Conducting zone vs respiratory zone: where do oxygen and carbon dioxide cross between air and blood?
cards.back: Only in the respiratory zone: the smallest airways with alveoli in their walls, and the alveoli themselves.
cards.why: The conducting zone, from the nose to the last airways without alveoli, only filters, warms, humidifies and carries air. Gas can cross only where the wall is thin simple squamous epithelium next to capillaries.

cards.front: Conducting zone vs respiratory zone: what lines each, and why?
cards.back: Conducting zone: mostly pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells. Respiratory zone: simple squamous epithelium, with no cilia or mucus.
cards.why: Thick, ciliated, mucus-covered lining traps and clears particles; the thinnest possible lining lets gases diffuse fast. Each zone’s lining fits its job.

cards.front: Is the whole upper respiratory tract conducting zone or respiratory zone?
cards.back: All of it is conducting zone, and so is much of the lower tract.
cards.why: The upper and lower tracts divide the airway by place; the two zones divide it by job. No gas exchange happens anywhere above the smallest airways.

cards.front: Where does the mucociliary escalator carry mucus, and what happens to it?
cards.back: Cilia sweep it backward from the nasal cavity and upward from the trachea and the air tubes of the lungs, to the pharynx, where it is swallowed.
cards.why: Trapped particles and microbes end up in the stomach, where acid destroys them. Smoke slows and destroys the cilia, leaving coughing as the only way to clear mucus.

cards.front: Vocal folds vs vestibular folds: which pair makes sound, and which lies higher?
cards.back: The lower pair, the true vocal cords (vocal folds), vibrate to make sound. The upper vestibular folds (false vocal cords) do not.
cards.why: The vocal folds hold an elastic ligament and small muscles that tighten them, and their stratified squamous lining withstands vibrating hundreds of times a second. Both pairs help seal the airway.

cards.front: Which is the only complete ring of cartilage in the airway?
cards.back: The cricoid cartilage, just below the thyroid cartilage.
cards.why: The rings that hold the trachea open below it are C-shaped, open at the back where the esophagus lies.

cards.compare: Type I vs type II alveolar cells
cards.front: Type I vs type II alveolar cells: what is the main job of each?
cards.back: Type I: form the thin wall that gases cross. Type II: secrete surfactant, the lipid-protein film that lowers surface tension.
cards.why: Type I cells are simple squamous and spread extremely thin; type II cells are cuboidal, with the machinery to make and secrete surfactant.

cards.compare: Type I vs type II alveolar cells
cards.front: Type I vs type II alveolar cells: which covers more of the alveolar surface, and which is more numerous?
cards.back: Type I cells cover about 95% of the surface; type II cells are more numerous but cover only about 5%.
cards.why: Each type I cell spreads into a huge, thin sheet, so a few of them cover most of the area. Type II cells are small and cuboidal.

cards.compare: Type I vs type II alveolar cells
cards.front: After the alveolar wall is injured, which cells replace lost type I cells?
cards.back: Type II alveolar cells, which divide and turn into new type I cells.
cards.why: Type I cells rarely, if ever, divide, so repair depends on type II cells.

cards.front: Why does an inhaled peanut usually lodge in the right primary bronchus?
cards.back: The right primary bronchus is wider, shorter and more nearly vertical than the left.
cards.why: The left bronchus angles further sideways to pass under the aortic arch and around the heart, so objects fall more directly into the right.

cards.front: Pulmonary vs bronchial circulation: which carries oxygenated blood in its arteries, and what is it for?
cards.back: The bronchial arteries, from the systemic circuit, carry oxygenated blood to feed the airway walls, connective tissue and visceral pleura.
cards.why: The pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to be loaded with oxygen in the alveolar capillaries; the bronchial arteries supply the lung’s own tissue.

cards.front: How does the thin film of pleural fluid make the lungs follow the chest wall?
cards.back: A thin liquid film between two smooth surfaces lets them slide but resists pulling them apart, so the lung surface moves out with the chest wall.
cards.why: Like two wet panes of glass: easy to slide, hard to separate. Let air into the gap between the layers and the lung no longer follows.

cards.front: By Boyle’s law, why does air flow in when the diaphragm contracts?
cards.back: The chest and lungs enlarge, so alveolar pressure falls below atmospheric (to about −1 mm Hg), and air flows down that gradient.
cards.why: For a fixed amount of gas, a larger volume means a lower pressure: the same molecules strike the walls less often.

cards.front: Alveolar vs intrapleural pressure: which returns to atmospheric whenever airflow stops?
cards.back: Alveolar pressure. Intrapleural pressure stays below atmospheric, about −4 to −6 mm Hg, throughout quiet breathing.
cards.why: The alveoli connect to the outside through the airways, so their pressure evens out when flow stops. The sealed pleural film is pulled between the inward-recoiling lung and the outward-springing chest wall.

cards.front: Which muscles power a quiet breath out?
cards.back: None: quiet expiration is passive. The stretched lungs recoil and the relaxed muscles let the chest settle.
cards.why: Energy stored in the stretched elastic fibers during inspiration pushes the air out. Forced expiration adds the internal intercostals and abdominal wall muscles.

cards.front: What does surfactant do to lung compliance, and why?
cards.back: It raises compliance by lowering the surface tension of the fluid lining the alveoli.
cards.why: Surface tension accounts for more than half of the lungs’ resistance to stretch. Surfactant phospholipids push between water molecules at the surface and weaken their pull.

cards.front: Bronchoconstriction vs bronchodilation: which signal causes each?
cards.back: Constriction: acetylcholine from the vagus nerve on muscarinic receptor proteins, and histamine and leukotrienes from mast cells. Dilation: epinephrine on beta-2 receptor proteins.
cards.why: Human airway smooth muscle gets few sympathetic fibers, so circulating epinephrine is the main dilator, which is why injected epinephrine opens the airways in a severe allergic reaction.

cards.front: Why does a pneumothorax usually collapse only one lung?
cards.back: Each lung has its own pleural cavity, so the seal on the other side stays intact.
cards.why: Only a tension pneumothorax, where trapped air pushes the mediastinum across, threatens the other lung and the heart.

cards.front: Obstructive vs restrictive disease: what is the basic problem in each?
cards.back: Obstructive: narrowed airways, so air has trouble getting out. Restrictive: the lungs or chest cannot expand fully, so air has trouble getting in.
cards.why: Airway resistance rises steeply as radius falls, which slows the breath out. Stiff lungs, a stiff or loaded chest wall, or weak muscles limit how far the lungs fill.

cards.front: Obstructive vs restrictive disease: what happens to the FEV1/FVC ratio?
cards.back: Obstructive: low, below about 0.70. Restrictive: normal or high.
cards.why: In obstruction air leaves slowly, so FEV1 falls far more than FVC. In restriction the volume is small, but the open airways let it out quickly.

cards.front: Obstructive vs restrictive disease: what happens to total lung capacity and residual volume?
cards.back: Obstructive: TLC normal or raised, residual volume raised (air trapping). Restrictive: TLC low, which defines restriction.
cards.why: Narrowed airways close early during a forced breath out and trap air behind them. Restriction is confirmed only by a measured TLC, because spirometry cannot see the residual volume.

cards.front: Which volumes add up to vital capacity?
cards.back: Tidal volume + inspiratory reserve volume + expiratory reserve volume (about 500 + 3,000 + 1,200 = 4,700 mL).
cards.why: Vital capacity is the most you can breathe out after the deepest breath in, so it includes every volume except the residual volume, which never leaves.

cards.front: Why can’t a spirometer measure residual volume, FRC or total lung capacity?
cards.back: They all include the residual volume, which never passes the mouthpiece.
cards.why: A spirometer measures only air that crosses the mouth. Helium dilution or a sealed body box (using Boyle’s law) is needed.

cards.front: Why do fast, shallow breaths deliver less fresh air than slow, deep ones at the same minute ventilation?
cards.back: About 150 mL of every breath only fills the dead space, so more breaths pay that cost more often.
cards.why: Alveolar ventilation = (tidal volume − dead space) × rate: 24 breaths of 250 mL give 2.4 L/min, but 6 breaths of 1,000 mL give 5.1 L/min.

cards.front: External vs internal respiration: where does each happen?
cards.back: External: between alveolar air and blood in the pulmonary capillaries. Internal: between blood in systemic capillaries and the tissue cells.
cards.why: Both are simple diffusion down partial pressure gradients; only the direction of each gas differs.

cards.front: External vs internal respiration: which way does oxygen move in each?
cards.back: External: from air into blood (PO2 100 → 40). Internal: from blood into cells (PO2 95 → 40 or lower).
cards.why: Cells use oxygen and make carbon dioxide, so the gradients in the tissues run opposite to those in the lungs.

cards.front: How is internal respiration different from cellular respiration?
cards.back: Internal respiration is gases crossing between blood and cells; cellular respiration is the chemistry inside the cell that uses the oxygen and makes the carbon dioxide.
cards.why: Internal respiration adjusts itself: a cell using oxygen faster lowers its PO2, which steepens the gradient and draws more oxygen from the blood.

cards.front: Air on a high mountain is still about 21% oxygen. Why is its PO2 lower?
cards.back: Partial pressure = total pressure × fraction. The total pressure is lower, so oxygen’s share is lower.
cards.why: At 4,300 m, moist airway air has a PO2 of about 85 mm Hg instead of 150: (455 − 47) × 0.209.

cards.front: Why can a carbon dioxide gradient of only 6 mm Hg move as much gas as an oxygen gradient of 60?
cards.back: Carbon dioxide is about 20 times more soluble than oxygen.
cards.why: Rate depends on gradient × solubility: 6 × 20 = 120 against 60 × 1, so carbon dioxide crosses about twice as readily.

cards.front: Systemic vs pulmonary arterioles: how does each respond to low PO2?
cards.back: Systemic arterioles dilate; pulmonary arterioles constrict (hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction).
cards.why: Systemic dilation brings more blood to tissue short of oxygen. Pulmonary constriction sends blood away from poorly ventilated alveoli toward well-ventilated ones, matching blood flow to airflow.

cards.front: In what two forms does blood carry oxygen, and in what shares?
cards.back: Bound to hemoglobin, about 98.5%; dissolved in plasma, about 1.5%.
cards.why: Plasma dissolves only 0.3 mL per 100 mL at a PO2 of 100 mm Hg. The small dissolved share still sets the PO2, which decides how much hemoglobin loads.

cards.front: Right shift vs left shift of the dissociation curve: what happens to P50 and to oxygen released?
cards.back: Right: P50 rises and more oxygen is released. Left: P50 falls and less is released.
cards.why: A right shift lowers hemoglobin’s affinity, so saturation is lower at any tissue PO2; a left shift raises affinity.

cards.front: Which four factors shift the dissociation curve to the right?
cards.back: More carbon dioxide, more H+ (lower pH), higher temperature and more 2,3-BPG.
cards.why: Each is higher in active tissue, so hemoglobin unloads more where oxygen is needed. Memory aid: “CADET, face right.”

cards.front: Name two causes of a left shift besides less carbon dioxide, fewer H+ and cooler blood.
cards.back: Fetal hemoglobin and carbon monoxide (also less 2,3-BPG, as in stored blood).
cards.why: Fetal hemoglobin binds 2,3-BPG weakly; carbon monoxide holds hemoglobin in its relaxed, high-affinity shape.

cards.front: Why does breathing extra oxygen add almost nothing to hemoglobin in a healthy person at sea level?
cards.back: At a PO2 of 100 mm Hg hemoglobin is already about 98% saturated, on the flat top of the curve.
cards.why: The flat top also protects loading when PO2 falls, for example at moderate altitude: at 60 mm Hg saturation is still about 90%.

cards.front: In carbon monoxide poisoning, why are arterial PO2 and SpO2 both misleadingly normal?
cards.back: PO2 measures only dissolved oxygen, which is normal; a standard oximeter reads carboxyhemoglobin as oxyhemoglobin.
cards.why: The oxygen content is low and the curve is shifted left. A CO-oximeter, using several wavelengths, measures carboxyhemoglobin directly.

cards.front: Which type of hypoxia has a normal arterial PO2 and oxygen content but a high venous PO2?
cards.back: Histotoxic hypoxia, as in cyanide poisoning.
cards.why: Oxygen arrives but the cells cannot use it, so it stays in the blood. In stagnant hypoxia, slow flow lets tissues strip more oxygen, and venous PO2 falls instead.

cards.front: In what three forms does blood carry carbon dioxide, and roughly what shares?
cards.back: Bicarbonate about 70%, carbaminohemoglobin about 20 to 23%, dissolved about 7 to 10%.
cards.why: Only the dissolved form sets PCO2 and crosses membranes, but most is converted to bicarbonate inside red blood cells, thanks to carbonic anhydrase.

cards.front: Bohr effect vs Haldane effect: what changes in each?
cards.back: Bohr: carbon dioxide and H+ lower hemoglobin’s affinity for oxygen. Haldane: less oxygen on hemoglobin lets the blood carry more carbon dioxide.
cards.why: They are the same chemistry seen from opposite sides: binding H+ and carbon dioxide at some sites lowers hemoglobin’s hold on oxygen, and binding oxygen lowers its hold on them.

cards.front: What is the chloride shift, and why is it needed?
cards.back: Band 3 swaps one bicarbonate out of the red blood cell for one chloride in.
cards.why: Bicarbonate building up inside would slow its own formation. The one-for-one swap moves it into the plasma without changing the charge across the membrane, and uses no ATP.

cards.front: Arterial PCO2 rises. Which way does blood pH go, and why?
cards.back: Down: CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3− is pushed to the right, releasing hydrogen ions.
cards.why: Because carbon dioxide leaves only through the lungs, breathing can change blood acid within minutes.

cards.front: Central vs peripheral chemoreceptors: what does each mainly sense?
cards.back: Central: hydrogen ions made from carbon dioxide in the brain’s fluid. Peripheral: low PO2, and also high PCO2 and low pH of arterial blood.
cards.why: Carbon dioxide crosses the blood–brain barrier and forms acid in poorly buffered fluid. Only the peripheral chemoreceptors respond to low oxygen.

cards.front: Central vs peripheral chemoreceptors: where is each, and how does its signal reach the medulla?
cards.back: Central: near the front surface of the medulla oblongata, with short connections in the brainstem. Peripheral: carotid bodies (glossopharyngeal nerves) and aortic bodies (vagus nerves).
cards.why: The carotid bodies sit at the fork of each common carotid artery and are the main peripheral chemoreceptors in humans.

cards.front: Central vs peripheral chemoreceptors: which responds faster, and which supplies most of the response to carbon dioxide?
cards.back: Peripheral chemoreceptors respond within seconds; central chemoreceptors are slower but supply most of the steady response, roughly two thirds to four fifths.
cards.why: Carbon dioxide takes tens of seconds to minutes to change the pH of the brain’s fluid, but it acts on a large, sensitive population of central neurons.

cards.front: Why does breathing barely change when arterial PO2 falls from 95 to 60 mm Hg?
cards.back: The carotid bodies fire only weakly until arterial PO2 drops below about 60 mm Hg, then steeply.
cards.why: That is the shape of the carotid bodies’ own response curve. Meanwhile hemoglobin stays about 90% saturated or more over that range, so little oxygen is lost. Carbon dioxide is the minute-to-minute drive: a rise from 40 to 45 mm Hg roughly doubles ventilation.

cards.front: Hyperventilation vs hypoventilation: what defines each?
cards.back: Arterial PCO2: below 35 mm Hg is hyperventilation; above 45 mm Hg is hypoventilation.
cards.why: The terms compare ventilation with carbon dioxide production, not breathing rate. Rapid, shallow breathing can be hypoventilation, because much of each breath only fills the dead space.

cards.front: How does hyperpnea in exercise differ from hyperventilation?
cards.back: In hyperpnea ventilation rises to match metabolism, so arterial PCO2 stays normal; in hyperventilation PCO2 falls.
cards.why: During moderate exercise, arterial PCO2, PO2 and pH hardly change, so the chemoreceptors are not what drives the rise; central command and limb proprioceptors are.

cards.front: Giving a lot of oxygen to some people with long-term carbon dioxide retention raises their PCO2. What is the better-supported cause?
cards.back: Worsening ventilation–perfusion mismatch (oxygen reverses hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction) plus the Haldane effect.
cards.why: Loss of a “hypoxic drive to breathe” plays at most a small part. For your exam: many EMT and nursing materials still give hypoxic drive; know it, but never withhold oxygen from a hypoxic patient.

cards.compare: Emphysema vs chronic bronchitis vs asthma
cards.front: Emphysema vs chronic bronchitis vs asthma: where is the main problem in each?
cards.back: Emphysema: the alveolar walls. Chronic bronchitis: the bronchi and bronchioles. Asthma: the bronchi and bronchioles.
cards.why: All three are obstructive, but emphysema destroys the tissue that holds small airways open, while the other two narrow the airway lumen itself.

cards.compare: Emphysema vs chronic bronchitis vs asthma
cards.front: Emphysema vs chronic bronchitis vs asthma: which obstruction largely reverses with a drug that opens the airways?
cards.back: Asthma, especially between attacks. Chronic bronchitis reverses little and emphysema not at all.
cards.why: A bronchodilator relaxes smooth muscle. It cannot restore destroyed elastic fibers or clear thickened, mucus-filled walls.

cards.compare: Emphysema vs chronic bronchitis vs asthma
cards.front: Emphysema vs chronic bronchitis vs asthma: which raises lung compliance and lowers gas diffusion?
cards.back: Emphysema.
cards.why: Losing elastic fibers makes the lungs stretch more easily, and losing alveolar walls removes surface area and its capillaries. Compliance and diffusion stay near normal in the other two.

cards.compare: Emphysema vs chronic bronchitis vs asthma
cards.front: Which of the three is defined by symptoms: a cough bringing up mucus on most days for at least three months in two years in a row?
cards.back: Chronic bronchitis.
cards.why: Enlarged mucus glands and extra goblet cells make far more mucus, and damaged cilia cannot clear it.

cards.front: Cardiogenic vs noncardiogenic pulmonary edema: what goes wrong in each?
cards.back: Cardiogenic: pressure in the pulmonary capillaries rises, as in left-sided heart failure. Noncardiogenic: the capillary wall and respiratory membrane become leaky.
cards.why: That is why cardiogenic edema fluid is low in protein and noncardiogenic fluid is high in protein.

cards.front: Latent TB infection vs active TB disease: which one spreads to others?
cards.back: Only active TB of the lungs or airways. In latent infection the bacteria are held in check inside granulomas and cause no symptoms.
cards.why: Active TB can develop later if immunity weakens, for example with HIV, some cancer treatments, diabetes or old age.

cards.front: Every lung disorder breaks at least one of four steps. What are they?
cards.back: Ventilation, diffusion, matching of air to blood (V/Q), and control of breathing.
cards.why: Ask which step a disease breaks, then follow its effects through the gases, the pH, the heart and the blood.

cards.front: CNS vs PNS: what does each include, and what is each one’s main job?
cards.back: CNS: brain and spinal cord; integration. PNS: nerves, ganglia and sensory receptors; carrying signals in to the CNS and out from it.
cards.why: Integration needs neurons contacting one another in large numbers, which happens in the brain and cord; the PNS is the wiring that links them to every part of the body.

cards.front: Sensory (afferent) vs motor (efferent) division: which way does each carry signals, and what happens if its axons are cut?
cards.back: Afferent: toward the CNS; cutting it causes numbness. Efferent: away from the CNS to effectors; cutting it causes weakness or paralysis.
cards.why: A signal is felt only when it reaches the CNS, and an effector acts only when a command reaches it, so each loss follows the direction the axons carry.

cards.front: Somatic vs autonomic nervous system: what are the effectors of each?
cards.back: Somatic: skeletal muscle. Autonomic: cardiac muscle, smooth muscle and glands.
cards.why: The dividing line is the effector, not whether you decide: shivering uses skeletal muscle, so it is somatic even though it is involuntary.

cards.front: Somatic vs autonomic: how many neurons link the CNS to the effector, and can the output inhibit?
cards.back: Somatic: one motor neuron, and it always excites. Autonomic: a chain of two neurons meeting in a ganglion, and it can excite or inhibit.
cards.why: A somatic motor neuron always makes skeletal muscle contract; autonomic effects depend on the organ and the branch, so the same system can speed one organ and slow another.

cards.front: Gray matter vs white matter: what does each contain, and where does each sit in the brain and the spinal cord?
cards.back: Gray: cell bodies, dendrites and axon terminals, where integration happens. White: bundles of insulated axons. Brain: gray outside. Spinal cord: gray inside.
cards.why: White matter is pale because of the fatty glial wrapping around its axons; gray matter has little of it and many cell bodies.

cards.front: What is a cluster of neuron cell bodies called in the CNS and in the PNS? And a bundle of axons?
cards.back: Cell bodies: a nucleus in the CNS, a ganglion in the PNS. Axons: a tract in the CNS, a nerve in the PNS.
cards.why: The names change at the border of the CNS: one sensory axon runs in a nerve, has its cell body in a ganglion, and continues in a tract.

cards.front: Does the CNS handle conscious actions and the PNS automatic ones?
cards.back: No. CNS vs PNS is a split by location; somatic vs autonomic is a split by function, and each has parts in both locations.
cards.why: The neurons that decide to speed your heart sit in the brain, and the axons that carry the command run in nerves of the PNS, just as for moving your leg.

cards.front: Dendrites vs axon: which way does each carry signals, and what kind of electrical signal does each carry?
cards.back: Dendrites: toward the soma, graded potentials. Axon: away from the soma, action potentials.
cards.why: Dendrites receive at synapses and their membrane has few voltage-gated sodium channels; the axon’s membrane has the channels to fire and regenerate action potentials.

cards.front: Where on a neuron do action potentials start, and why there?
cards.back: In the initial segment, just beyond the axon hillock: the trigger zone. (Many exams name the axon hillock.)
cards.why: Its membrane is packed with voltage-gated sodium channels, many times more densely than the soma’s, so it reaches threshold first.

cards.compare: Multipolar vs bipolar vs unipolar neurons
cards.front: Multipolar, bipolar and unipolar neurons: how many processes leave the soma, and what job does each usually do?
cards.back: Multipolar: many; motor neurons and interneurons. Bipolar: two; sensory, in a few sense organs. Unipolar: one that splits in two; most sensory neurons.
cards.why: Shape follows job and position: a unipolar sensory neuron’s signal runs past its soma, which sits off to one side in a ganglion.

cards.compare: Sensory neuron vs interneuron vs motor neuron
cards.front: Sensory neurons, interneurons and motor neurons: where does each carry signals, and which is the most numerous?
cards.back: Sensory: from sensory receptors to the CNS. Interneurons: between neurons within the CNS, the vast majority. Motor: from the CNS to effectors.
cards.why: Integration is the interneurons’ job, and nearly all processing happens within the CNS, so they far outnumber the neurons that carry signals in or out.

cards.front: CNS glia vs PNS glia: which cell makes myelin on each side?
cards.back: CNS: oligodendrocytes. PNS: Schwann cells.
cards.why: Both wrap layers of their own membrane around axon segments, but an oligodendrocyte serves many axons and a Schwann cell only one segment of one.

cards.front: CNS glia vs PNS glia: which cells surround neuron cell bodies and regulate the fluid around them?
cards.back: CNS: astrocytes. PNS: satellite cells, which cover the somas in ganglia.
cards.why: Neurons fire correctly only when the ions around them stay steady; these glia take up excess potassium and neurotransmitter.

cards.front: CNS glia vs PNS glia: which cells clear debris and fight infection?
cards.back: CNS: microglia, the resident immune cells. PNS: Schwann cells, with macrophages that arrive from the blood.
cards.why: Microglia come from immune precursor cells that settle in the brain early in development, which is why they behave like macrophages.

cards.front: Which glial cells line the fluid-filled spaces inside the brain and spinal cord, and do they have a PNS equivalent?
cards.back: Ependymal cells; there is no PNS equivalent.
cards.why: Only the CNS has fluid-filled cavities, left from the hollow of the embryo’s tube; many ependymal cells carry cilia that help move the fluid.

cards.front: Schwann cell vs oligodendrocyte: how many axons does each myelinate, and which has a neurilemma?
cards.back: Schwann cell: one segment of one axon, with its nucleus in an outer living layer, the neurilemma. Oligodendrocyte: segments of many axons, and no neurilemma.
cards.why: The Schwann cell’s living outer layer is what lets it multiply and guide a regrowing axon after an injury.

cards.front: What is a node of Ranvier?
cards.back: A tiny bare gap, about a thousandth of a millimeter wide, between two myelin segments, where voltage-gated sodium channels are packed densely.
cards.why: Each glial wrap covers only one internode, so the axon membrane is exposed between wraps; those gaps are where the action potential is regenerated.

cards.compare: PNS axon cut vs CNS axon cut
cards.front: Why can a cut axon in the PNS regrow, while one in the CNS rarely does?
cards.back: PNS: Schwann cells clear debris fast and form a guiding tube. CNS: no guiding tube, growth-blocking myelin proteins that linger, and an astrocyte scar.
cards.why: CNS neurons can grow axons into a graft of peripheral nerve, so the problem is mainly the surroundings, not the neurons themselves.

cards.front: About how fast does a cut PNS axon regrow, and why does feeling return near the scar first?
cards.back: About 1 mm a day, so a 20 cm distance takes six months or more; feeling returns from the repair outward.
cards.why: The growing tip advances along the Schwann cell tube at roughly the speed of slow axonal transport, reaching nearby targets long before distant ones.

cards.front: Why do most tumors that start in brain tissue arise from glial cells rather than neurons?
cards.back: Mature neurons do not divide; glial cells and their precursors keep dividing.
cards.why: A tumor is cells dividing out of control, which only cells that still divide can do.

cards.front: Voltage-gated sodium vs potassium channels in an axon: how many gates, how fast do they open, and what ends the flow?
cards.back: Sodium: two gates (activation and inactivation), opens fast; the inactivation gate plugs it. Potassium: one gate, opens slowly; it closes slowly after repolarization.
cards.why: That timing difference shapes the spike: fast sodium entry makes the rise, and slow potassium exit makes the fall and the dip below rest.

cards.front: Name the three states of a voltage-gated sodium channel, and say how an inactivated channel returns to ready.
cards.back: Closed (ready), open and inactivated. It resets to closed only when the membrane repolarizes.
cards.why: Repolarization swings the activation gate shut and lets the inactivation gate swing out of the pore; while the membrane stays depolarized, that cannot happen.

cards.front: Absolute vs relative refractory period: can a second action potential fire, and why?
cards.back: Absolute: no, whatever the stimulus, because every sodium channel is open or inactivated. Relative: yes, but only with a stronger-than-normal stimulus.
cards.why: In the relative period some sodium channels have reset, but fewer are ready and the still-open potassium channels hold the membrane below rest.

cards.front: Is the refractory period the time the sodium–potassium pump needs to restore the ions?
cards.back: No. It comes from the sodium channels, which inactivate and cannot reset until the membrane repolarizes.
cards.why: One action potential moves only a tiny fraction of the ions, and the pump works slowly in the background.

cards.front: Give the four key voltages of a neuron action potential.
cards.back: Rest about −70 mV; threshold about −55 mV; peak about +30 mV; afterhyperpolarization about −80 mV.
cards.why: The peak stops short of sodium’s equilibrium potential (+60 mV) because inactivation and the potassium channels cut the rise off; the dip heads toward potassium’s (−90 mV).

cards.front: Continuous vs saltatory conduction: in which axons, and where is the action potential regenerated?
cards.back: Continuous: unmyelinated axons, at every patch of membrane. Saltatory: myelinated axons, only at the nodes of Ranvier.
cards.why: Under myelin there are few sodium channels and little current leaks out, so the slow step, a patch firing, happens only at the nodes.

cards.front: Continuous vs saltatory conduction: typical speed and energy cost?
cards.back: Continuous: about 0.5 to 2 m/s, higher cost. Saltatory: about 5 to 120 m/s, lower cost.
cards.why: Ions cross only at the nodes in a myelinated axon, so the sodium–potassium pumps have far less to restore after each signal.

cards.front: What three things set an axon’s conduction velocity?
cards.back: Axon diameter, myelination (the bigger effect) and temperature.
cards.why: A wider axon has less internal resistance, myelin stops current leaking out between nodes, and warm channels open and close faster.

cards.front: Why does a hot shower briefly worsen the symptoms of multiple sclerosis?
cards.back: Warmth makes sodium channels inactivate sooner, so each action potential carries less current, and a demyelinated axon that barely reached threshold at the next node now fails.
cards.why: A healthy axon has current to spare; a demyelinated one leaks current across its bare stretch, so the small loss tips it into conduction block.

cards.front: Why does a modest rise in blood potassium make neurons more excitable, but a severe, lasting rise make them less?
cards.back: Modest: the resting potential moves closer to threshold. Severe and lasting: the held depolarization leaves sodium channels stuck inactivated, raising threshold.
