cards.why: Carbonic anhydrase makes H<sup>+</sup> and HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> together; the H<sup>+</sup> goes to the lumen and the bicarbonate to the blood, until pancreatic bicarbonate secretion balances it.

cards.front: Why do chief cells make pepsinogen instead of pepsin?
cards.back: Pepsinogen is an inactive zymogen, so it can be stored without digesting the cell’s own proteins.
cards.why: It becomes pepsin only in acid below about pH 5, and pepsin then activates more pepsinogen: positive feedback.

cards.front: Which secretion of the stomach can you not live without?
cards.back: Intrinsic factor.
cards.why: Without it you absorb almost no vitamin B12. A person without a stomach digests food well with small meals but needs B12 replacement for life.

cards.compare: Cephalic vs gastric vs intestinal phase
cards.front: Cephalic vs gastric vs intestinal phase: where is the stimulus?
cards.back: Cephalic: head (sight, smell, taste, thought, chewing). Gastric: stomach (stretch, protein, rising pH). Intestinal: first part of the small intestine (acid, fat, stretch).
cards.why: The phases are named for where the stimulus is, not where the secretion happens.

cards.compare: Cephalic vs gastric vs intestinal phase
cards.front: Which phase of gastric secretion supplies most of the acid, and which mostly inhibits?
cards.back: The gastric phase supplies about half or more; the cephalic about a third. The intestinal phase mostly inhibits.
cards.why: In the intestinal phase, the enterogastric reflex, secretin and CCK act as the brake on the stomach.

cards.front: Rank carbohydrate, protein and fat by how fast they leave the stomach.
cards.back: Carbohydrate fastest, protein slower, fat slowest.
cards.why: Fat releases the most CCK, and CCK weakens the antrum’s waves and tightens the pylorus.

cards.front: What makes up the gastric mucosal barrier?
cards.back: Alkaline mucus with bicarbonate, tight junctions, renewal of the surface cells every 3 to 5 days, mucosal blood flow, and prostaglandins.
cards.why: Together they keep the cell surface near pH 7 while the lumen, less than a millimeter away, is near pH 1 to 2.

cards.front: What causes most peptic ulcers?
cards.back: Helicobacter pylori infection and NSAIDs, both of which weaken the mucosal barrier.
cards.why: Ulcers usually form because the barrier fails, not because acid secretion is high. Stress and spicy food are not causes.

cards.front: In vomiting, what supplies the force?
cards.back: The diaphragm and abdominal muscles contracting together; the stomach and lower esophageal sphincter are relaxed.
cards.why: The relaxed stomach is squeezed between them. Repeated vomiting loses H<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup> and leads to alkalosis and low potassium.

cards.front: Jejunum vs ileum: how do their walls and folds differ?
cards.back: Jejunum: thicker, wider, redder, with tall close circular folds, tall villi and few Peyer’s patches. Ileum: thinner, paler, with low sparse folds, shorter villi and many Peyer’s patches.
cards.why: The jejunum does most nutrient absorption, so its surface is largest; the ileum’s many lymphoid nodules guard the approach to the bacteria-rich large intestine.

cards.front: Which jobs belong to the ileum alone?
cards.back: Absorbing vitamin B12 bound to intrinsic factor and recovering most of the bile secreted during a meal for reuse.
cards.why: The carriers and receptor proteins for both are found only in the terminal ileum, so no other part can take over.

cards.front: How long is the small intestine in a living adult?
cards.back: About 3 to 5 meters. After death, when its muscle loses tone, it measures about 6 meters.
cards.why: Living muscle keeps some tone and shortens the tube. Exams may still give the older 6 m (20 ft) figure.

cards.front: How large is the absorptive surface of the small intestine, and how much do folds, villi and microvilli multiply it?
cards.back: About 30 m², roughly 100- to 200-fold a smooth tube. The textbook estimate is 3 × 10 × 20 = 600-fold, or 200 to 300 m².
cards.why: Direct measurements in the living intestine found smaller multipliers than the old estimates; exams may still expect the tennis-court figure.

cards.front: What carries absorbed nutrients away inside a villus?
cards.back: Blood capillaries take sugars, amino acids and water; a central lacteal takes absorbed fat.
cards.why: Fat is packaged into droplets too large for blood capillaries, so it enters the lymphatic lacteal instead.

cards.front: Why does cancer chemotherapy so often damage the gut?
cards.back: Stem cells in the intestinal glands divide constantly to replace the lining every 3 to 5 days, and chemotherapy kills dividing cells.
cards.why: The intestinal lining is one of the fastest-renewing tissues in the body.

cards.front: Is intestinal juice rich in digestive enzymes?
cards.back: No. It is 1 to 2 L a day of watery, slightly alkaline fluid with mucus and very little enzyme.
cards.why: Its job is to keep chyme fluid. The last digestive cuts are made by brush border enzymes fixed in the microvillus membrane.

cards.front: Lactase, sucrase, maltase: substrate and products?
cards.back: Lactase: lactose to glucose and galactose. Sucrase: sucrose to glucose and fructose. Maltase: maltose to two glucose.
cards.why: Each is named for its substrate, and each sits in the microvillus membrane beside the carriers that absorb its products.

cards.front: When the villi are damaged, which brush border enzyme is usually the first to fall?
cards.back: Lactase.
cards.why: It is the least abundant of them, so losing cells shows first as lactase shortage; it recovers when the lining heals.

cards.front: Segmentation vs migrating motor complex: when, trigger, and job?
cards.back: Segmentation: during and after a meal, driven by chyme stretching the wall; mixes. Migrating motor complex: between meals, every 90 to 120 minutes, driven by motilin; sweeps residue and bacteria into the large intestine.
cards.why: Eating stops the migrating motor complex at once, and segmentation takes over again.

cards.front: What share of the liver’s blood comes from the hepatic portal vein, and what share from the hepatic artery?
cards.back: About three quarters from the hepatic portal vein, about a quarter from the hepatic artery.
cards.why: Portal blood is rich in absorbed nutrients but partly deoxygenated; the artery supplies oxygenated blood.

cards.front: In a liver lobule, which way do blood and bile flow?
cards.back: Blood flows inward, from the portal triads through the sinusoids to the central vein. Bile flows outward, through the canaliculi to the bile ducts in the triads.
cards.why: The two run in opposite directions in separate channels and never mix.

cards.front: Does bile digest fat?
cards.back: No. Bile has no enzymes. Its bile salts emulsify fat into tiny droplets, multiplying the surface pancreatic lipase can act on.
cards.why: A bile salt has a hydrophobic face in the fat and a hydrophilic face in the water, which stops droplets merging again.

cards.front: Does the gallbladder make bile?
cards.back: No. It stores and concentrates it, up to about tenfold, by absorbing sodium and letting water follow.
cards.why: Between meals the closed hepatopancreatic sphincter backs bile up the cystic duct into the gallbladder; CCK empties it after a meal.

cards.front: A gallstone blocks the common bile duct. Name three signs.
cards.back: Jaundice with dark urine, pale feces, and fat in the feces.
cards.why: Conjugated bilirubin backs up into the blood and urine instead of reaching the gut, and without bile salts fat is poorly emulsified.

cards.compare: Secretin vs CCK on the pancreas
cards.front: Secretin vs CCK: which pancreatic cells does each target, and what juice results?
cards.back: Secretin: duct cells; a large volume rich in bicarbonate, with few enzymes. CCK: acinar cells; a small volume rich in enzymes.
cards.why: Each hormone calls for what removes its own stimulus: bicarbonate for acid, enzymes for fat and protein.

cards.compare: Secretin vs CCK on the pancreas
cards.front: Secretin vs CCK: effect on the gallbladder and the hepatopancreatic sphincter?
cards.back: CCK contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the sphincter. Secretin has little direct effect on either.
cards.why: Bile is needed for fat, and fat is CCK’s stimulus, not secretin’s.

cards.front: Why is the pancreas not digested by its own trypsin?
cards.back: It makes trypsinogen, an inactive zymogen, which is switched on only by enteropeptidase on the duodenal brush border.
cards.why: The acinar cells also make a trypsin inhibitor, and their secretions keep flowing out of the gland. In acute pancreatitis, trypsin is activated inside the gland.

cards.front: How is making pancreatic bicarbonate the mirror image of making stomach acid?
cards.back: Pancreatic duct cells put bicarbonate into the duct and H<sup>+</sup> into the blood; parietal cells put H<sup>+</sup> into the stomach and bicarbonate into the blood.
cards.why: So blood leaving the stomach after a meal is slightly alkaline (the alkaline tide), and blood leaving the pancreas slightly acidic.

cards.front: Hepatitis vs cirrhosis: what is each?
cards.back: Hepatitis: inflammation of the liver, acute or long-lasting. Cirrhosis: scarring that replaces normal lobules with scar bands and nodules, after years of injury.
cards.why: Long-lasting hepatitis from any cause can end in cirrhosis.

cards.front: Can cirrhosis get better?
cards.back: Partly. Scarring can regress once the cause is removed, as when hepatitis C is cured, but the liver seldom returns fully to normal.
cards.why: Cirrhosis that has already caused complications regresses least; hepatitis often recovers fully once its cause is gone.

cards.front: Which cells lay down the scar in cirrhosis?
cards.back: Hepatic stellate cells, star-shaped cells just outside the sinusoid lining, once activated by repeated injury.
cards.why: They are not the macrophages of the sinusoids; activated, they make collagen.

cards.front: Why does cirrhosis cause bleeding veins at the lower esophagus?
cards.back: Scar squeezes the sinusoids, pressure in the hepatic portal vein rises, and blood backs up into veins linking the portal system to the systemic veins, which swell and can rupture.
cards.why: Portal vein pressure is raised in cirrhosis but usually normal in hepatitis.

cards.front: Small vs large intestine: surface of the lining and goblet cells?
cards.back: Small: circular folds, villi and microvilli; goblet cells present. Large: no circular folds or villi, a flat surface with deep glands; very many goblet cells.
cards.why: Nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine, which needs the surface; the colon needs mucus to lubricate drying feces and keep bacteria off its cells.

cards.front: Small vs large intestine: outer longitudinal muscle and main movements?
cards.back: Small: a continuous layer; segmentation after meals and the migrating motor complex between them. Large: three teniae coli that gather it into haustra; slow haustral contractions and a few mass movements a day.
cards.why: The teniae coli are shorter than the colon wall, so their tone bunches it into pouches.

cards.front: Small vs large intestine: how much water does each absorb a day?
cards.back: Small intestine: about 7 to 8 L. Large intestine: about 1.3 L, around 90% of what reaches it.
cards.why: The colon’s share is small, but it is the last chance, so any change in it shows in the stool.

cards.front: Small vs large intestine: length, width, and time contents spend there?
cards.back: Small: about 3 to 5 m in life, 2.5 cm wide, 3 to 5 hours. Large: about 1.5 m, 6 to 7 cm wide, 12 to 48 hours or longer.
cards.why: “Small” and “large” refer to width, not length.

cards.front: Small vs large intestine: enzymes and bacteria?
cards.back: Small: brush border enzymes plus pancreatic juice and bile; relatively few bacteria. Large: no digestive enzymes of its own; trillions of bacteria do the breaking down.
cards.why: Stomach acid and fast flow keep bacteria sparse higher up; the slow, oxygen-poor, fiber-rich colon lets them thrive.

cards.front: Do bacteria outnumber your own cells ten to one?
cards.back: No: roughly 38 trillion bacteria and 30 trillion human cells, about one to one.
cards.why: A careful recount in 2016 replaced the old ten-to-one estimate, though some exams still expect it.

cards.front: What do colon bacteria make from fiber, and why does it matter?
cards.back: Short-chain fatty acids (acetate, propionate, butyrate) and gases. Butyrate is the main fuel of the colon’s epithelial cells.
cards.why: You have no enzymes for most fiber, so bacterial fermentation recovers some of its energy, roughly 5 to 10% of your daily energy.

cards.front: How does the colon absorb water, with no water pump?
cards.back: It absorbs sodium through apical channels, pumps it out with sodium–potassium pumps, chloride follows, and water follows by osmosis.
cards.why: Aldosterone adds channels and pumps, so the colon saves more sodium and water when your body is low on them.

cards.front: Internal vs external anal sphincter: muscle, control and nerves?
cards.back: Internal: smooth muscle, involuntary, autonomic and enteric nerves; relaxes by reflex when the rectum stretches. External: skeletal muscle, voluntary, somatic motor neurons from the sacral cord.
cards.why: The reflex opens the internal sphincter; the external one stays closed until you decide to relax it.

cards.front: A spinal cord injury above the sacral segments: what happens to defecation?
cards.back: The reflex still works, but the person no longer feels the urge or controls the external anal sphincter.
cards.why: The reflex arc runs through the sacral cord (S2–S4); the injury cuts only the path to and from the brain.

cards.front: Diarrhea vs constipation: time in the colon and water absorbed?
cards.back: Diarrhea: time usually shortened, less water absorbed. Constipation: time usually lengthened, more water absorbed.
cards.why: The colon keeps absorbing water for as long as contents stay, so time decides how hard the stool is.

cards.front: Diarrhea vs constipation: main danger?
cards.back: Diarrhea: loss of water, sodium, potassium and bicarbonate. Constipation: discomfort and, rarely, a blockage of hard stool.
cards.why: Stool water carries potassium, which the colon secretes, and bicarbonate, so severe diarrhea lowers blood volume and potassium and makes the blood more acidic.

cards.front: Secretory vs osmotic diarrhea: mechanism and example?
cards.back: Secretory: a toxin makes the lining secrete chloride, and sodium and water follow (cholera). Osmotic: an unabsorbed solute holds water in the lumen (magnesium laxatives, sorbitol).
cards.why: Either way, more water stays in the lumen than the colon can take back.

cards.compare: Digestive enzymes by source, substrate and product
cards.front: Salivary and pancreatic amylase: substrate and products?
cards.back: Starch and glycogen, split into maltose, maltotriose and α-dextrins.
cards.why: Amylase cannot cut the bond at a branch point, so α-dextrins keep their branches until brush border α-dextrinase splits them.

cards.compare: Digestive enzymes by source, substrate and product
cards.front: Pepsin vs trypsin, chymotrypsin and elastase: source and products?
cards.back: Pepsin: stomach chief cells; large polypeptides. Trypsin, chymotrypsin, elastase: pancreas; shorter peptides.
cards.why: Each cuts inside the chain, at bonds next to particular amino acids; peptidases then finish the pieces.

cards.compare: Digestive enzymes by source, substrate and product
cards.front: Carboxypeptidase vs aminopeptidase: source, and which end does each trim?
cards.back: Carboxypeptidase: pancreas; removes amino acids from the carboxyl end. Aminopeptidase: brush border; removes them from the amino end.
cards.why: Trimming from both ends, with dipeptidase splitting dipeptides, leaves single amino acids and short peptides.

cards.compare: Digestive enzymes by source, substrate and product
cards.front: Gastric vs pancreatic lipase: products and share of fat digestion?
cards.back: Gastric: fatty acids and diglycerides, a small share (roughly 10 to 30% in adults). Pancreatic: fatty acids and monoglycerides, most of it.
cards.why: Pancreatic lipase works on bile-emulsified droplets, anchored to their surface by colipase.

cards.compare: Digestive enzymes by source, substrate and product
cards.front: How are DNA and RNA from food digested?
cards.back: Pancreatic ribonuclease and deoxyribonuclease cut them into nucleotides; brush border nucleosidases and phosphatases split those into pentose sugars, nitrogenous bases and phosphate.
cards.why: Every cell you eat contains nucleic acids, and only these small parts can be absorbed.

cards.front: SGLT1 uses no ATP. Why does stopping the sodium–potassium pumps stop glucose absorption?
cards.back: The pumps keep sodium low inside the cell; SGLT1 is powered by sodium running down that gradient. Without the pumps, the gradient collapses.
cards.why: This is secondary active transport: the energy comes from the ATP the pumps spent, one step removed.

cards.front: How do glucose, galactose and fructose enter and leave an absorptive cell?
cards.back: Glucose and galactose enter with sodium through SGLT1; fructose enters by facilitated diffusion through GLUT5. All three leave through GLUT2.
cards.why: Each membrane has its own carriers, and that difference makes absorption run one way.

cards.front: Are dietary proteins absorbed only as single amino acids?
cards.back: No: much crosses the brush border as dipeptides and tripeptides, carried with hydrogen ions and split inside the cell. Almost all reaches the blood as amino acids.
cards.why: Many textbooks and exams still say "absorbed as amino acids", which is true of what enters the blood.

cards.front: Micelle vs chylomicron: where does each form, and what is its job?
cards.back: Micelle: in the lumen; carries digested lipids to the brush border. Chylomicron: inside the absorptive cell; carries absorbed lipids out of the cell.
cards.why: Micelles need bile salts and release their lipids at the membrane; chylomicrons are rebuilt triglycerides packaged for export.

cards.front: Where do chylomicrons go, and why not into the blood capillaries?
cards.back: Into the lacteal, then the lymph, the thoracic duct and the veins where the left internal jugular and subclavian veins meet.
cards.why: They are tens to hundreds of times wider than a micelle, too large for blood capillaries, so absorbed fat reaches the blood without passing the liver first.

cards.front: Name four organs vitamin B12 absorption depends on.
cards.back: Stomach (acid, pepsin, intrinsic factor), pancreas (proteases that free it from haptocorrin), terminal ileum (receptor proteins), and liver (stores 3 to 5 years’ worth).
cards.why: A break anywhere causes deficiency, but only years later because of the liver’s store. High oral doses let a small fraction cross without intrinsic factor.

cards.front: About how much water passes through the gut each day, and how much leaves in the feces?
cards.back: About 9 L in (about 2 L from food and drink, 7 L from secretions); about 150 mL leaves in the feces, so about 98% is absorbed.
cards.why: Water in = water absorbed + water in the feces. Gastric juice alone is about 2 L a day.

cards.front: Why does an oral rehydration solution need glucose as well as salt?
cards.back: Cholera toxin does not stop SGLT1, so glucose carries sodium into the cells, and water follows, even while secretion continues.
cards.why: Salt alone is absorbed poorly when the gut is secreting; coupling sodium to glucose opens a route the toxin leaves intact.

cards.front: Lactose intolerance vs milk allergy: cause and molecule?
cards.back: Intolerance: too little lactase to digest lactose, a sugar; no immune response. Allergy: an immune response, often IgE-mediated, to milk proteins such as casein.
cards.why: Intolerance depends on the dose and small amounts are usually tolerated; in an allergy even tiny amounts can trigger a reaction.

cards.front: Why does undigested lactose cause gas and diarrhea?
cards.back: It holds water in the lumen by osmosis, and colon bacteria ferment it into hydrogen, carbon dioxide and fatty acids.
cards.why: The gas causes bloating and flatus; the water and extra solutes cause osmotic diarrhea. The absorbed hydrogen is what the breath test detects.

cards.front: Where does the thoracic duct return absorbed fat to the blood?
cards.back: At the left venous angle, where the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins meet.
cards.why: Chyle climbs from the cisterna chyli through the thoracic duct, so absorbed long-chain fat bypasses the liver on its first pass.
